subject: Business Models
title: The Rise of Advertising
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Rise of Advertising.

hook.text: In 1920, people bought what they needed. By 1960, advertising taught them to want what they didn't.

buildup.text: Radio and TV gave brands direct access to millions of homes. The ad agency era began.

discovery.text: Ads shifted from product features to emotions. You weren't buying soap—you were buying confidence.

twist.text: Advertising costs are passed to consumers. Every product's price includes its marketing budget.

climax.text: The ad-supported model funds most media. News, TV, and social media all run on attention.

punchline.text: If it's free, you're the product. Ads pay for everything.

quiz.question: How did advertising evolve from 1920 to 1960?

details.summary: Modern advertising emerged in the late 1800s as mass production created products that needed mass demand. Newspapers, magazines, radio, and television became dependent on advertising revenue, creating the attention economy where media exists primarily to deliver audiences to advertisers.
details.whyItMatters: Advertising fundamentally reshaped commerce by separating product value from perceived value. It created the concept of brand premium, funded the entire media industry.
takeaways: Mass production required mass demand creation, driving the need for advertising
Media became financially dependent on advertising revenue rather than audience payments
Advertising created the attention economy model that now dominates internet business

faq.question: How did advertising change the relationship between products and consumers?
faq.answer: Before advertising, products competed primarily on function and price. Advertising created emotional associations, lifestyle aspirations, and brand loyalty that justify premium pricing. Consumers began choosing products based on identity and aspiration rather than just utility and cost.

faq.question: Why did the advertising model come to dominate media?
faq.answer: Advertisers pay more per consumer than consumers will pay directly for content. This makes ad-supported media cheaper or free for consumers while generating higher total revenue than subscriptions alone. The model creates a three-sided market of content creators, audiences, and advertisers.
